newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban forces make gains as Iran hosts talks.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban forces make gains as Iran hosts talks.

text.p: The forces of a northern alliance have pushed back the Taleban militia in fighting in the remote northwest of Afghanistan, reliable sources said on Tuesday.
Iran opened a conference in Tehran to seek a solution to the Afghan crisis, but Pakistan, a key player in neighbouring Afghanistan, stayed away from the talks.

The Taleban, who took Kabul a month ago, have said their forces captured Badghis province on the border with Turkmenistan late last week and were driving on Maimana, capital of neighbouring Faryab province.
Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference on Tuesday that Badghis was calm and "big changes will happen in the north in the very near future".
"The majority of commanders in the north have close links with the (Taleban) Islamic state. An uprising will start in the north and Dostum will be engulfed," Mutaqi said.
But reliable sources said 2,000 men dispatched by northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum to meet the threat on a new front had counter-attacked successfully.

The Kabul-based sources, who have contacts with the region, said Dostum forces led by General Malik, who uses only one name, captured the town of Bala Morghab, some 60 km (40 miles) inside Badghis province on Sunday.
"Yesterday, there was fighting near Qalaye-i-Naw," said one source of the Badghis capital another 80 km (50 miles) into the province. "Our information is that General Malik is still advancing."

If Dostum could recapture Badghis, he would be in a position to threaten the western city of Herat where there is a big population of ethnic Tajiks, cousins to the people of Dostum ally Ahmad Shah Masood, the ousted government military chief.
It could also open up the southern plains and allow the northern alliance to threaten Kandahar, the southern city where the Taleban have their headquarters.
Such a threat might force the Taleban to weaken their defensive line north of Kabul, where the front line has been static for a week, Afghan watchers in Kabul said.
Masood and Dostum have made repeated attempts to overcome Taleban defensive lines in hills snaking across the plain 25-30 km (15-19 miles) north of the capital.
Taleban fighters at the front said the combined forces of the alliance tried again on Monday night but were repulsed.
There was no immediate confirmation of the report, but witnesses said the front lines had not changed.
Reuters correspondent Chris Bird reported that Masood's forces were bringing up more rocket batteries to the front.

In Tehran, Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati opened the two-day regional conference and said he hoped it could lay the ground for an international conference aimed at bringing peace and reconstruction to Afghanistan.

He said the United Nations had not done enough to draw attention to the plight of the Afghan people and urged the world body to stop the intervention of "foreign countries in Afghanistan's internal affairs".

He was apparently referring to Pakistan, which the Iranian media have accused of setting up the Sunni Moslem Taleban with backing from the United States and funding from Saudi Arabia to counter Iran's influence in the region.
Pakistan, which plays an active role in Afghanistan, denies the charge and says it has no favourites among Afghan factions.
Although invited to the two-day conference, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Uzbekistan did not send delegates.
Pakistan said it would not attend, citing problems with the agenda and guest list, which includes arch-foe India.

The conference was attended by delegates from the United Nations, Russia, China, India, Turkey, the Organisation of the Islamic Conference as well as Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
Journalists in Tehran said Velayati told a news conference that Ireland sent an official to represent the European Union.
